# The Strange Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about how we're taught to complete things. Finish your plate. Finish your homework. See projects through to completion. There's wisdom in that—follow-through matters. But I wonder if we've overcorrected, turning incompleteness into something shameful.

Some of my favorite books are ones I never finished. Not because they were bad, but because I loved them exactly as they were in my imagination—the story continuing somewhere in that space between the final page I read and the ones I skipped. The ending I invented was probably messier and more honest than what the author wrote.

I have a sketchbook half-filled with drawings that trail off into white space. A handful of hobbies I picked up and never mastered. Conversations with friends that ended mid-thought because life happened. These gaps don't feel like failures anymore. They feel like breathing room.

There's something almost rebellious about accepting that you don't need to optimize every corner of your life into productivity and closure. Not everything deserves an ending. Some things are better as sketches—suggestion and potential matter more than definition.

I think the Japanese have it right with their concept of *ma*—the negative space that gives meaning to what surrounds it. The silence between notes makes the music. The blank wall makes the painting.

We're so focused on the architecture we build that we forget emptiness isn't absence. It's possibility. And maybe that's worth leaving alone sometimes.
